content: Between 2012 and October 17, 2022, a total of 2,600 laboratory-confirmed cases of Middle East Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus (MERS-CoV) were reported to the World Health Organization (WHO). Of these, 84% (2,193 cases) were reported from Saudi Arabia. MERS cases have been documented in 27 countries across the Middle East, North Africa, Europe, the United States, and Asia. To date, 935 deaths have been attributed to MERS, resulting in a crude case fatality rate of 36%. The majority of cases (69%) were male, with a median age of 58 years (range: 23–98 years). Retrospective reporting from Qatar identified three additional cases from 2017, including one death. Among cases reported since July 2019, 81% had at least one underlying condition, such as chronic renal failure, heart disease, diabetes mellitus, or hypertension. Only 5% of these cases were asymptomatic or had mild disease, a lower proportion compared to the 22% reported in the previous global summary in 2019. This reduction likely reflects decreased testing and case detection during the COVID-19 pandemic rather than a change in the virus's virulence. The epidemiology, transmission patterns, clinical presentation, and viral characteristics of MERS-CoV remain consistent with previous observations. MERS-CoV is a zoonotic virus that primarily enters the human population through direct or indirect contact with infected dromedary camels in the Arabian Peninsula. Human-to-human transmission has occurred among close contacts and in healthcare settings, though it remains limited outside of these environments. WHO anticipates additional MERS cases will be reported, particularly as surveillance activities resume. Cases may also be exported to other countries by individuals exposed to infected camels, camel products (e.g., raw camel milk), or infected humans, particularly in healthcare settings. Since the last update in 2019, several small MERS clusters have been reported. These include household clusters in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, and Doha, Qatar, as well as nosocomial clusters in Abha, Wadi Aldwasir, and Al Kharj, Saudi Arabia. Nosocomial clusters often involved healthcare workers (HCWs) who provided care to infected patients. While some clusters resulted in fatalities, others did not. Zoonotic transmission of MERS-CoV continues to be a concern. Improvements in multi-sectoral investigations of community-acquired cases have been noted, including testing of dromedary camels and follow-up of human contacts. Investigations in camels are conducted by agricultural officials, and positive results are reported to the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH). Human-to-human transmission of MERS-CoV remains limited, with most cases occurring in healthcare settings. Despite being a relatively rare disease, MERS often goes unrecognized due to its non-specific symptoms, which range from asymptomatic to severe respiratory distress. Globally, 2,600 laboratory-confirmed MERS cases have been reported since 2012, with a median age of 53 years and 69% of cases being male. Approximately 20% of cases had no or mild symptoms, while 48% experienced severe disease or died. Underlying conditions such as diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, chronic renal failure, or lung disease were reported in 53% of cases, with over 70% of fatal cases having at least one of these conditions. MERS cases have been reported in 27 countries, with Saudi Arabia accounting for 84% of cases. Healthcare workers are at higher risk of MERS-CoV infection, with at least 17% of cases involving HCWs. The largest outbreak outside the Middle East occurred in South Korea in 2015, resulting in 186 cases and 39 deaths. Early suspicion, isolation, and clinical management of cases have been effective in preventing further transmission. The basic reproduction number (R0) of MERS-CoV is generally less than 1, though it can exceed 1 in healthcare settings. WHO expects additional cases to be reported, particularly in the Middle East, as zoonotic transmission from camels continues. Full genome sequencing is recommended for cases involving contact with camels or clusters of human cases. WHO continues to update guidance materials and collaborate with international partners to address MERS-CoV. The risk of MERS-CoV recombination with SARS-CoV-2 is considered remote, but field investigations are ongoing. Control of MERS-CoV requires national leadership, coordination between animal and human health sectors, public trust, and clear communication. WHO is working with FAO and WOAH to better understand MERS-CoV dynamics at the animal-human interface using a One Health approach.
